summary: A reply to RFC 86, which proposed a standard way to send graphics over the network. The author at Ames Research Center agrees that sending a device-independent description and converting it at the receiving host is sound. The main objection is that the proposal ignores many features of real graphics devices.

eli5.summary: Instead of mailing a drawing already made for one printer, you mail instructions that any machine can follow. The writer likes the idea but says it forgets about some fancy tools.

questions: is a device-independent graphics format a good idea
what were the objections to rfc 86
what is a network graphics data stream
subtitle: A 1971 reply to the graphics data stream proposal: sound idea, but add modes, richer text and picture interaction.

tldr.problem: RFC 86 proposed a network standard format for a graphics data stream, but the author felt it ignored the many features of real graphics devices.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes separate mode primitives, form control characters in strings, a display list pointer, an include list primitive, list manipulation commands and ways to report what a user points at.
tldr.outcome: It is a set of comments rather than a specification, and it asks for more discussion of how a user interacts with a displayed picture.

today: RFC 125 updates RFC 86 and is updated by RFC 177, according to the unit metadata. It is a set of comments, and the text does not say that its proposals were adopted.

sections.title: Support for the Approach
sections.content:
John McConnell of Ames Research Center writes in response to RFC 86. He says that sending an intermediate, device-independent language that the receiving host translates into specific device codes is sound, and that it appears to be the only approach that lets people focus on picture descriptions.

Ames Research Center had adopted the approach to tie its graphics facilities together. At the time of writing it was in the design phase and expected its package to be running in about six months.
sections.eli5: The writer agrees that sending picture instructions, not finished pictures, is a good plan, and says his own lab is already trying it.

sections.title: Modes and Character Strings
sections.content:
The main objection is that the structure takes no account of the many features of graphics devices. The memo proposes mode primitives, logically separate from the drawing primitives of RFC 86. A mode applies until another mode primitive resets it, and an interpreter can treat a mode as a null operation if the feature is missing. Modes could control intensity levels, colour, blinking and, for vectors, dashed lines.

For character strings, the memo takes strong exception to excluding form control characters. It lists backspace (BS), new line (LF), shift case (SO/SI), superscript (DC2), subscript (DC4), a special non-ASCII character (DC3) and tab. It also asks for size and orientation options, and a way to define symbols not in ASCII, either with a control code and a 16-bit list name or by allowing 8-bit characters.
sections.eli5: Drawing commands should stay simple, with separate switches for extras like colour or blinking. Words should be able to carry little signals for things like tiny raised letters.

sections.title: Display Lists and Manipulation
sections.content:
The memo adds a display list pointer (NGDLP) whose value is a displacement from the head of a list and names the next drawing primitive to run. When an execute list primitive is met, the current pointer is saved with the list name and current origin, and restored when the list finishes.

An include list primitive would treat a sub-list like a macro rather than a subroutine, so that changing one sub-list does not change every sub-picture. To cut data volume, extra commands would let the receiving host rescale, translate the origin, rotate, show or hide a list, or enable or disable light pen detection without a retransmission.
sections.eli5: A bookmark tracks which drawing step comes next, and you can copy a small picture into a big one. You can also shrink, move or turn a picture without sending it all again.

sections.title: Interacting with the Picture
sections.content:
The memo says interaction with the displayed picture has not yet been addressed. Keyboards and function keys are easy, since they can be sent as a standard message. Light pens, mice, joysticks and tablets are harder, because the point selected must be tied to a meaningful list or primitive, and this should be done at the receiving host.

To identify the object pointed at, the stack of suspended lists and the current pointer value would qualify it at any level of the hierarchy, together with normalized x,y coordinates and a character displacement if a string was pointed at. Where no beam motion occurs, a sub-list run periodically might be needed to find the light pen.
sections.eli5: Pointing at a picture is tricky, because the computer has to work out which thing you meant. The writer asks others to help think about it.

references.text: Osanna, J., Sahzer, J., "Remote Terminal Character Stream Processing of Multics", Proceedings SJCC, 1970, p. 671.
RFC 86, the proposal for a network standard format for a graphics data stream that this memo answers.
